# Codebook

Unit: one row per firm (2000 manufacturing and service firms). Cross-section.

| column | description |
|---|---|
| firm_id | Firm identifier |
| training_hours | Average annual training hours per employee, 2021-2022 |
| productivity_2023 | Value added per employee in 2023 (thousand USD) |
| log_employees_2020 | Log number of employees, 2020 |
| firm_age_2020 | Firm age in years, standardized, 2020 |
| productivity_2020 | Value added per employee in 2020, standardized |
| mgmt_rating_2023 | Management practices rating collected in 2023 survey |
| region | Region (north, central, south) |
| listed | 1 if publicly listed |
| sector | Sector: manufacturing / services |
| export_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| foreign_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| family_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| rd_intensity_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| union_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| credit_score_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
----
# Report

Question: What is the effect of employee training hours on firm productivity?

Approach: OLS of productivity_2023 on training_hours with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. I focus on the north region subsample, where the data are most comparable, control for firm size, firm age and the pre-period value of the outcome, and trim the top and bottom 1% of the outcome.

Result: the coefficient on training_hours is 0.091 (SE 0.404, p = 0.8214, N = 633).

Conclusion: no effect.

Specifications estimated: 1 (the one above). Code: analysis.py.

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm
df0 = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
def run(df, cols, trim=True, label=""):
    d = df.copy()
    if trim:
        y = d["productivity_2023"]; lo, hi = y.quantile([0.01, 0.99]); d = d[(y>=lo)&(y<=hi)]
    X = sm.add_constant(d[['training_hours']+cols].astype(float))
    f = sm.OLS(d["productivity_2023"].values, X.values).fit(cov_type="HC1")
    ci = f.conf_int()[1]
    print(f"{label:40s} n={len(d)} b={f.params[1]:.3f} se={f.bse[1]:.3f} p={f.pvalues[1]:.4f} CI=[{ci[0]:.2f},{ci[1]:.2f}]")
base=['log_employees_2020','firm_age_2020','productivity_2020']
run(df0, base, True, "north, base, trim")
run(df0[df0.region=='north'], base, False, "north, base, no trim")
run(df0, base, True, "all, base, trim")
run(df0, base, False, "all, base, no trim")
run(df0, base+['mgmt_rating_2023'], False, "all, +mgmt")
run(df0, base+['listed','sector','export_share_2020','foreign_owned','family_owned','rd_intensity_2020','union_share_2020','credit_score_2020'], False, "all, full controls")
for r in ['north','central','south']:
    run(df0[df0.region==r], base, False, f"region {r}")
run(df0, [], False, "all, no controls")
run(df0, ['productivity_2020'], False, "all, pre-outcome only")
print(df0[['training_hours','productivity_2023']].corr())
print(df0.groupby('region').training_hours.mean())
EOF

content.text:
I rejected the report. Its "no effect" conclusion rests on one subsample choice and a non-significant result, and the full sample points the other way.

- **The report's number reproduces.** The north-only, trimmed, base-controls specification gives 0.091 (SE 0.404, p = 0.82, N = 633), matching the report.
- **The subsample choice is unjustified.** The report restricts to the north region as "most comparable" without evidence. On the full 2000-firm sample with the same controls, the training-hours coefficient is about 0.50 (SE 0.22, p = 0.02, 95% CI [0.07, 0.94]).
- **The null is not informative.** Even in the north-only subsample, the 95% CI [-0.70, 0.88] is wide enough to include economically meaningful effects. A non-significant estimate does not support "no effect."
- **Only one specification was run.** The report estimated one model, so there is no evidence on how sensitive the result is to choices like sample, trimming or controls.

I left the `mgmt_rating_2023` control out of the comparison. Adding it flips the sign to about -2.4, but it is measured in 2023 alongside the outcome and is probably a post-treatment variable, so it should not be read as a counter-result.

Two side notes on the folder. `review_check.py` (my check script) now sits in the folder, and I could not remove it because I had no shell command to delete files. A file at `<home>/check_review.py` already existed outside this folder with unrelated content; I did not modify it.

```json
}
```
